k: AI UX  /  Conversational and agentic AI
Designing an AI that acts for people, and earns the right to

A B2B platform’s AI assistant was moving from answering questions to taking action: building workflows, changing and deleting people’s work, managing access and sending e-signature requests. I designed how it does that safely across three phases, from a single assistant to a model for team agents.
Interaction model, trust patterns, all flows, agent experience
All three phases designed by me, built by engineering
Letting an AI act on people’s work without it ever doing something they didn’t mean, couldn’t see coming, or weren’t allowed to do themselves.
Designed a trust model that scales with risk, the conversational patterns that apply it, and an agent model for teams, built on one design system.
23 user stories turned into one consistent experience, built by engineering. In testing with 20 people, 18 completed every task without help, and all 20 could follow what the assistant was doing.

k.i: Cover: the assistant proposing a plan before it acts (blur product names)

k: In its first phase, the assistant built workflows and answered questions. The next step gave it real power over people’s work: creating, changing and deleting items, changing who has access to a space, and contacting people outside the company.

Every one of those actions is something a person might regret. A misread name deletes the wrong item. A role change locks a colleague out, and they aren’t in the conversation to object. An e-signature request can’t be un-sent. Speed is the reason to use an assistant, and trust is the reason people keep using it.
Not a chatbot, a system of trust
The question wasn’t how the chat should look. It was: when should an AI act, what must people see first, and what happens when it can’t, or shouldn’t?
Reading a list carries no risk. Deleting 12 items, changing someone’s access, or sending a legal document carries a lot. One confirmation style can’t serve both.
Statuses follow allowed transitions, comments and activity logs are different places, files have versions, and permissions differ per space. An AI that ignores them quietly breaks the product.
The product’s surface is huge, so the assistant would always be able to do some things and not others. People needed to know which, before hitting the edge mid-task.
People were already struggling to find and build
Before designing, I gathered what the people closest to users kept seeing: feedback from internal users, sales and support, and patterns in product demos and support tickets.
Four problems came up again and again. Each one shaped a part of the design.
From internal users, sales and support
People didn’t know which step to use
In the workflow builder, people couldn’t tell which building block would get them the workflow they wanted.
Describe the workflow in plain words, and the assistant drafts it with the right steps, plus an “Explain a step” starter.
Workflows got built with the wrong building blocks, so they didn’t do what was intended and had to be fixed later.
A preview of the real steps before anything is created, so a wrong step is caught in the plan, not after it runs.
From internal users, sales and support
With so many spaces, people found it hard to find one or even remember its name. Asking the assistant made it much easier.
Plain-language finding with no confirmation for reads, and “Which one did you mean?” when names repeat.
People spent a long time searching for spaces and the items inside them before they could start the actual work.
Reads answer immediately as a short summary or table, with follow-ups to narrow down instead of browsing.
03  My role and how I led

I led the experience design of the assistant across all three phases: the interaction model, the trust patterns, every flow, and the agent experience. The product manager owned the specs; engineering built all three phases from my designs.
How the assistant asks, plans, confirms, explains and fails; every flow end to end; the agent selection and configuration experience; the AI components in the design system.
How the specs’ risk rules became visible behaviour, with the product manager; what the system could honestly promise, with engineering, through regular design reviews.
The written specs, the AI model and its prompts, or the build. Being clear about that kept decisions clean.
How I worked through the scope change

I had already designed separate agents when the product team decided Phase 2 should keep a single assistant. Instead of discarding that work, I redesigned it into visible tool steps for Phase 2 and carried the agent designs forward as the foundation of Phase 3, which I then designed in full. Engineering built every phase from these designs and the AI components in the design system.
Raising the bar beyond my own screens
A trust model only works if everyone building the product follows it. So a big part of my role was making it the team’s shared standard, not just my design.
Design reviews with product and engineering
I ran reviews with the product manager and engineers, checking each flow against the trust model and against what the backend could honestly promise, before anything was built.
I wrote the confirmation tiers as usable rules, the AI guidelines, and the AI components in the design system. Product and engineering used them to decide how every new action should behave.
Mentoring the team and shaping what came next
I mentor a team of 8 designers and coached them on designing for AI. My work also shaped the roadmap, including carrying the agent designs forward into Phase 3.
Being the bridge between users and engineering

I made sure I understood both sides: what users struggled with, and what the technology could and couldn’t do. When answers were slow or sometimes wrong, I turned those technical limits into design responses, a loader people could follow and honest messages when something didn’t work, so engineering’s constraints became better experiences instead of hidden problems.
Earn autonomy one phase at a time
Rather than launching an all-powerful assistant, each phase gave it more power only once the trust patterns for that power were in place.

It also had to work within firm rules: people confirm in their own words, the assistant never has more power than the person using it, deletes can’t be undone, and separate agents were cut from Phase 2 halfway through, so the design had to absorb that.
Builds and edits workflows by conversation, and answers questions. Introduced visible progress, plans before changes and conversational confirmation.
An assistant that acts on work
Creates, updates and deletes work items, manages access, sends external requests and answers reporting questions, under a risk-tiered trust model.
Specialist agents people can create, train, share and deploy across the platform, with ownership, permissions and memory people can inspect.

I explored many directions before committing. Five questions drove the try-outs: where the assistant should live, how it should start a conversation, how it should look, whether people should be able to talk to it, and how agents should fit in.

k: Creating and managing your own agents

I first designed separate agents for workflows and work. Asking people to pick a specialist before they could ask anything added a decision to every conversation, and the product team chose to keep a single assistant for Phase 2. The agent work came back in Phase 3 in a stronger form: agents as teammates that teams create, train and share themselves.
One assistant first. Then specialist agents, including custom ones people build, with ownership, sharing and testing before they go live.
Every action is classified before it ships. The tier decides how much people see before the question. How they answer never changes: a plain reply in the chat.
Creating and updating items, comments, files, spaces
The exact plan; for updates, the current and new value of every field
“Would you like me to create this?”
Deletes, bulk deletes, access and roles, ownership, versions, automations
Exact count, sample names, who is affected, and that it can’t be undone
“Do you want me to delete these 12 items?”
E-signatures, identity checks, one-time codes, outbound email
Who is contacted, through which channel, that it leaves the platform and can’t be recalled
“Yes”, “Go ahead”, “Do it”: the action runs and a result confirms it.
“Ok?”, “Hmm”, “Wait”: nothing happens, and the assistant asks again.
“Yes, but only the first 3”: a new plan for 3, and a new question.
Five decisions, and what they cost
Each had real options and a real trade-off.
Screens are shown as built. Those tagged “Refined design” are improvements I designed after the build; see “What I’d improve next”.
Make the question carry the weight
Confirmation had to happen in words, with no buttons. A vague “Are you sure?” invites a careless yes.
A generic question; making people type an exact phrase; a specific question that names the action, the count and the consequence.
Every plan ends with a question that says exactly what will happen: “Do you want me to delete these 9 items?”, with names and “can’t be undone” shown just above it.
A little slower for confident users. Reads never ask, so the pause only appears when something changes.

k.i: A delete plan: count, names, “can’t be undone”, then the question
Three items with the same name, listed with their space and due date

k: Item names repeat across spaces, and support tickets already showed people struggling to find and remember them. A wrong guess on a delete can’t be reversed.
Pick the most likely match; ask after the plan; resolve everything before the plan.
When a name matches several items, the assistant lists them with enough context to tell them apart. Missing details are asked for in one message. Only then does it show a plan.
One more turn in the conversation, in exchange for a plan that is actually correct.
The same permissions as the person
The assistant could technically reach more than the person using it, and reporting could quietly count items from spaces they can’t open.
Trust the backend to reject; filter only writes; check every action and every number against the person’s own access.
Permission is checked before anything is attempted. A refusal names the missing permission in plain words. Totals only include what the person could see themselves, with a short note saying so.
Some answers are narrower than they could be, which is exactly the point.

Progress steps that name the product being used, and the greyed “Coming soon” panel

k: One assistant, with its work made visible
I had designed separate agents for workflows and work. After review, the product team decided the assistant should stay a single interface in Phase 2.
Keep pushing for agents; drop the work; turn agents into something people could still see and trust.

The assistant routes work behind the scenes and shows it as steps: “Using workflows”, “Using work items”. The reporting layer is never named. The agent designs weren’t thrown away: they became the starting point for Phase 3.

People lose the idea of choosing a specialist for now, but gain one simple place to ask. The same visible steps later became our answer to slow responses: a wait you can follow feels shorter than an empty one.
The worst AI failure isn’t a gap. It’s reporting success for something that never happened.
Hide failures behind a generic error; retry silently; give every kind of failure its own honest message.

Unsupported actions say so and point to where to do it. If someone else changed an item first, the assistant says what changed and does nothing. Charts fall back to text. “No data” is said in words, never shown as zero.
More states to design and maintain, and some honest “I can’t do that yet” moments.

k.i: A conflict message: “This changed before I could update it”

k: From an assistant to a team of agents

Phase 3 lets teams create specialist agents, like an HR or a finance agent, that remember context, can be trained on a team’s own documents, and can be reached across the platform. More power again, so more trust patterns.
Every agent has a name, avatar and status. Switching agents keeps the conversation and marks the change in the thread.
Test before anyone relies on it
Creators train an agent on documents, links and FAQs, see each source’s status, and test privately before publishing.
Owners can see what an agent has learned and remove individual entries, instead of trusting a black box.

What we saw with internal users
The assistant didn’t always get the answer right, which is the fastest way to lose trust in an AI that acts.
Golden conversations and an evaluation scorecard, so wrong answers are caught before each release, not by users.
Answers took time to arrive, and an empty wait made the assistant feel slow and uncertain.
A transparent loader in the latest design: live steps that say what the assistant is doing and how far along it is, so the wait feels purposeful.
When an answer came with suggested next questions, internal users tended to keep the conversation going instead of leaving.
Follow-up suggestions after every answer became a standard pattern in the design system.

All three phases were built by engineering from these designs. The four confirmation tiers became the rule every new action is classified against before it ships, so new capabilities follow the same trust model without a fresh design debate.
Usage alone doesn’t show trust. These measures do.
How often people change a plan before saying yes
Shows plans are read and are catching mistakes

The real test of whether people trust its results
Tested with 20 people: 15 internal users and 5 from outside the company
Six tasks each: building a workflow, changing it, checking progress, deleting with care, fixing a failed run and sharing an agent.

When an answer was bad, people used the feedback option to flag it rather than abandoning the conversation.
18 of 20 didn’t notice the note saying the numbers only include spaces they can access.
I moved it above the chart, so it’s read before the numbers.
Only 5 of 20 checked how many items would be deleted before confirming. Plans were being skimmed, the exact risk this design exists to prevent.
Next change: put the count and the first names into the question itself, “Delete these 9 items: Kickoff call, Vendor contacts and 7 more?”, so it can’t be skipped.
After the build, I reviewed the shipped screens against the trust model and found places where they didn’t yet live up to it. These are the changes I designed next.

The built progress card showed steps unrelated to the request, and long waits made it feel slow. The refined loader names only real steps, the product each one uses, and how far along it is, so people can follow the wait instead of staring at it.

k: Standards for how the assistant behaves
Screens show what the assistant looks like. Its behaviour, what it says and when, is decided in its instructions and only shows up in real answers.

When internal users tried it, answers were sometimes wrong. So I turned the trust model into three standards that guide how the assistant’s behaviour is written and tested, and catch wrong answers before release.

k.i: Voice and conversation guide

k: How it speaks, asks, confirms and reports, with a fixed pattern for every kind of failure.

k.i: 15 golden conversations

k: The ideal answer to the situations that matter most, including messy replies like “ok?” and changed requests.

k.i: An evaluation scorecard

k: 8 checks, 3 severity levels and 15 test cases run before every release. Critical failures must be zero.

Designing an AI that acts is less about the chat and more about the rules behind it: when to ask, what to show, and how to fail honestly. The scope change taught me to design patterns that survive a change in direction.
Test the typed confirmation with real users before build, and bring engineering into the trust model earlier, since so much of it depends on what the backend can promise.
